name: Chromium Oxide
notes: Chromium(III) oxide, about 99% Cr2O3: a very strong, refractory green colorant (it melts at about 2435 C / 4415 F). In oxidizing firings from about cone 6 up a little chromium vaporizes and can flash pink onto nearby tin-opacified glazes; with zinc it turns brown.
manufacturer: Various pigment producers (e.g. Lanxess Colortherm Green; the Huntsman/Venator G-4099 family, sold by Laguna as MCHRGR); Potterycrafts P3401 in the UK
hazards: Not classified (no signal word) on the Potterycrafts and Laguna/Huntsman SDSs; some EU notifiers add H317 (may cause skin allergy). Contains traces of hexavalent chromium (under 100 ppm), and heating in air can form a little more, so avoid breathing the dust and kiln fumes.

source.name: Potterycrafts Chromic Oxide P3401 Technical Data Sheet

name: Cobalt Oxide
notes: Black cobalt oxide, mostly Co₃O₄, sold as about 71–73% cobalt: in a glaze it counts as about 92.7% CoO, with about 6.3% oxygen lost in firing (Potterycrafts lists 95% Co₃O₄, 4% CoO and 0.9% NiO as the main impurity). Gives up that oxygen to become CoO at about 900–950 C (1650–1740 F) in air, lower in reduction. About 1.6 times as strong as cobalt carbonate (93% CoO against 58%). A very strong blue: 0.25% gives a clear blue, 1–1.5% a deep blue-black.
manufacturer: Potterycrafts Ltd (UK supplier; producer not named)
hazards: Danger (Potterycrafts SDS): H334 may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled; H412 harmful to aquatic life. Laguna's US SDS adds H302 harmful if swallowed, H317 skin sensitizer and H351 suspected of causing cancer; some EU SDSs list H350i (may cause cancer by inhalation). Avoid breathing the dust.

source.name: Potterycrafts Technical Data Sheet, Cobalt Oxide P3403

name: Cobalt carbonate
notes: A pink-purple basic cobalt carbonate with 45–47% cobalt, so about 58% CoO; the rest (about 42%) burns off as CO2 and water. It disperses more evenly than cobalt oxide; use about 1.5 times as much for the same blue.
manufacturer: Potterycrafts Ltd (UK supplier; producer not named)
hazards: Danger (Potterycrafts SDS, matching the EU harmonised classification): H302 harmful if swallowed; H332 harmful if inhaled; H317 may cause an allergic skin reaction; H334 may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled; H341 suspected of causing genetic defects; H350i may cause cancer by inhalation; H360F may damage fertility; H400/H410 very toxic to aquatic life.

source.name: Potterycrafts Technical Data Sheet, Cobalt Carbonate P3402

name: Copper oxide
notes: Black copper oxide, CuO, about 98% pure (78–79% copper). Melts at about 1326 C (2419 F), but in air first loses oxygen to Cu₂O from about 1010–1030 C. A strong, active flux that can make glazes run; copper becomes increasingly volatile above about 1025 C (1877 F) and can flash onto nearby ware, especially tin whites. Coarser than the carbonate, so it can speckle. Over about 5% can give black metallic surfaces unsuitable for food ware.
manufacturer: Potterycrafts Ltd (UK supplier; producer not named)
hazards: Warning (Potterycrafts SDS): H400 very toxic to aquatic life; the EU harmonised classification is H400 and H410. US SDSs (Laguna, from Phibro) give H302 harmful if swallowed. Copper fumes from hot kilns cause metal fume fever; vent the kiln.

source.name: Potterycrafts Technical Data Sheet, Black Copper Oxide P3405

name: Copper carbonate
notes: Basic copper carbonate, a green powder with 55–57% copper, so about 70% CuO; the rest (about 30%) leaves as CO₂ and water from about 290 C (554 F). It does not melt. Gives more even color than black copper oxide. An active flux; fumes from about 815 C (1500 F) and can flash onto nearby ware, especially tin whites.
manufacturer: Old Bridge Minerals, Inc. (Old Bridge Chemicals), Old Bridge, New Jersey
hazards: Warning (Ceramic Color & Chemical SDS 00909-A, 2024-09, sold through The Ceramic Shop): H302 harmful if swallowed; H332 harmful if inhaled; H319 causes serious eye irritation; H400/H410 very toxic to aquatic life.

source.name: Old Bridge Minerals product sheet, Copper Carbonate Technical Grade

name: Ilmenite
notes: A natural source of iron and titanium in glazes.

source.name: Theoretical formula

hazards: Not classified (CTM SDS 31/32; under 0.1% quartz); avoid breathing the dust.

name: Black iron oxide
relatedTo: Magnetite, magnetic iron oxide, red iron oxide
notes: Magnetite, Fe₃O₄, also sold as magnetic iron oxide; some grades are ground natural ore containing quartz. Older potters’ books list black iron as FeO, but ferrous oxide is not sold as a potter’s material. Gram for gram it gives about as much iron as red iron oxide. A strong flux in reduction. Often coarser than red iron oxide; sieve or ball-mill it to avoid specks.

source.name: Theoretical formula

hazards: Not classified (CTM SDS 66); avoid breathing the dust.

name: Yellow iron oxide
relatedTo: Red iron oxide, black iron oxide
notes: A hydrated form of iron oxide. Insoluble in water, very fine particles.

source.name: Theoretical formula

hazards: Not classified (CTM SDS 73, synthetic yellow iron oxide); avoid breathing the dust.

name: Yellow ochre
notes: A material with hydrated iron oxide and clay. Sometimes called limonite (as a mineral of iron oxide). Many also have manganese.

source.name: Theoretical formula

hazards: Danger (New Riverside Ochre SDS): natural ochre with 20–29% quartz (carcinogen category 1A by inhalation; can cause silicosis) and 1.5–4% manganese dioxide; avoid breathing the dust.

name: Manganese dioxide
notes: Potters’ manganese dioxide is ground ore, typically about 75% MnO₂ with iron oxide, silica and alumina, so it gives only about 61% MnO. Loses oxygen in stages as it heats, to Mn₂O₃ at about 450–600 C and Mn₃O₄ at about 750–1100 C; the gas can cause bubbles. Browns, and purples in alkaline glazes; a flux once dissolved in the melt. Manganese fumes at high temperatures, so vent the kiln.
manufacturer: Potterycrafts Ltd (UK supplier; ground Australian ore)
hazards: Warning (Potterycrafts SDS; also Laguna/Prince BrickOx SDS; EU harmonised): H302 harmful if swallowed; H332 harmful if inhaled. Ore grades may also contain crystalline silica. Manganese fumes at high temperatures, so vent the kiln.

source.name: Potterycrafts Technical Data, Manganese Dioxide (Pyrolusite) P3415

name: Nickel oxide, green
notes: Green nickel oxide is stoichiometric NiO, 78.5% nickel. It does not decompose or melt in the kiln (NiO melts at about 1955 C / 3550 F) and is refractory, so use small amounts; it gives muted greens, browns and greys, and blues or pinks in some bases.
manufacturer: Novamet Specialty Products Corp. (Lebanon, Tennessee)
hazards: Danger (Laguna nickel oxide SDS, GHS version 06/15): H317 may cause an allergic skin reaction; H334 may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled; H350 may cause cancer (EU: H350i, by inhalation); H372 causes lung damage through prolonged or repeated inhalation; H413 may cause long-lasting harm to aquatic life.

source.name: Novamet Green Nickel Oxide product sheet

name: Nickel oxide, black
notes: Black nickel oxide is NiO with a little extra oxygen (about 76.4–77.6% nickel), not true Ni2O3. It loses that oxygen and becomes green NiO at about 600–700 C (1100–1300 F), so in a glaze it behaves like green nickel oxide, giving about 2% less NiO per gram.
manufacturer: Novamet Specialty Products Corp. (Lebanon, Tennessee)
hazards: Danger (Laguna nickel oxide SDS, GHS version 06/15, which names calcined black nickel oxide grades A and F): H317 may cause an allergic skin reaction; H334 may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled; H350 may cause cancer (EU: H350i, by inhalation); H372 causes lung damage through prolonged or repeated inhalation; H413 may cause long-lasting harm to aquatic life.

source.name: Novamet High Purity Black Nickel Oxide product sheet

name: Praseodymium Oxide
notes: Pr₆O₁₁, the dark brown form that is sold. Counted here as Pr₂O₃, the form praseodymium takes in a glaze; the extra oxygen (3.1%) and up to 1% moisture count as loss on ignition. Does not melt in a kiln (about 2183 C); the 931 C often quoted is for the metal. A weak colorant: 5–8% gives lime to yellow greens, and it is mostly used in zircon-praseodymium yellow stains.
manufacturer: Rare-earth refiners (mainly in China); sold by chemical suppliers rather than potter suppliers
hazards: Low hazard, but SDSs disagree: Fujifilm Wako (2023) not hazardous under GHS; LTS (2023) Warning, H315, H319, H335 (skin, eye and respiratory irritation). Most ECHA notifiers do not classify praseodymium oxide.

source.name: Xinglu Chemical, praseodymium oxide product specification (99.9% grade)

name: Rutile
notes: Natural rutile milled for ceramics: about 95% TiO2 with small amounts of silica, zircon, vanadium, iron and chromium. Current US and UK grades have under 1% iron oxide, not the 9–10% often assumed. Used for tan to brown variegation, opacity and crystal growth, and with cobalt, copper or iron for broken colours.
manufacturer: TAM Ceramics (Niagara Falls, NY), Ruflux 61 milled rutile; Potterycrafts P3338 in the UK
hazards: TAM Ceramics SDS (2018): Warning, eye and skin irritant (Category 2; H319, H315); dust may irritate the airways. Potterycrafts SDS: not classified. The EU's Carc. 2 listing for inhaled TiO2 powder was annulled (2022, upheld 2025).

source.name: The Ceramic Shop, Rutile, Dark: typical chemical analysis (trade name Milled Ruflux 61, TAM Ceramics)

name: Titanium dioxide
notes: TiO₂. Added at about 2–10% (4% is typical) for variegation, opacity and crystal growth, and with iron or cobalt for broken colors. Also in the materials list as Titanium Oxide, for recipes that count it in the base.

source.name: Theoretical formula

hazards: Not classified under EU rules (KRONOS SDS, non-pigmentary grade; CTM SDS 26 agrees); avoid breathing the dust.

name: Vanadium oxide
notes: Vanadium pentoxide, V2O5, an orange-yellow powder, about 99% pure. It melts at 690 C (1274 F) and acts as a flux; alone it gives weak yellows to browns, and with tin oxide or zircon stronger yellows. Highly toxic: wear a respirator, avoid dust and vent the kiln.
manufacturer: US Vanadium LLC (Hot Springs, Arkansas); potter suppliers repack material from various producers
hazards: Danger. EU/GB harmonised classification: H301 toxic if swallowed, H330 fatal if inhaled, H335 respiratory irritation, H341 suspected of causing genetic defects, H350 may cause cancer, H361fd fertility and unborn child, H362 harm to breast-fed children, H372 lung damage from repeated exposure, H411 toxic to aquatic life. US SDSs give a slightly milder but still serious set (H302+H332, H319, H335, H341, H351, H361, H372, H411).

source.name: US Vanadium Product Specification MC4 Rev. 10, Vanadium Pentoxide (Technical Grade)

name: Tin oxide
notes: Stannic oxide, SnO₂, about 99.5% pure. Does not melt at glaze temperatures (it melts at about 1630 C / 2966 F); it stays suspended as fine particles, which makes the glaze opaque: 4–6% gives a semi-opaque white, 8–10% full opacity, and a warm white in low-fired majolica. Opacifies poorly in reduction and at cone 10, where it starts to dissolve. Helps develop copper reds in reduction; with a trace of chrome it turns pink.
manufacturer: Potterycrafts P3361 (physical data match Keeling & Walker Superlite, UK); Laguna in the US sells tin oxide from Oximet/Endeka (Italy)
hazards: Not classified (no signal word) on current SDSs (Potterycrafts 2025, Laguna 2014). Breathing the dust for years can cause stannosis, a benign lung condition.

source.name: Potterycrafts Tin Oxide P3361 Technical Data Sheet

name: Zirconium oxide
notes: Zirconium dioxide, ZrO₂ (zirconia). Rarely used raw in glazes: most recipes call for zircon (Zircopax, Superpax), which is zirconium silicate. Insoluble; opacifies as it stays unmelted at glaze temperatures, stiffens the melt and can reduce crazing.

source.name: Theoretical formula

hazards: Not classified (ATI zirconium oxide SDS, EU); avoid breathing the dust.

name: Zircon
relatedTo: Zirconium silicate, Zircopax, Superpax, Excelopax, Ultrox, Zircosil, zirconium oxide
notes: Zirconium silicate, ZrSiO₄: 67.2% ZrO₂ and 32.8% SiO₂. Sold as Zircopax, Superpax, Excelopax, Ultrox and Zircosil, which differ mainly in particle size. The usual opacifier: about 4–7% for semi-opaque, 8–15% or more for full opacity; 1–3% mainly hardens the glaze. Works in reduction, unlike tin oxide. Its silica counts toward the glaze.

source.name: Theoretical formula

hazards: Not classified (CTM zirconium silicate SDS 29; under 0.01% respirable crystalline silica); slightly radioactive (uranium 285–343 ppm, thorium 116–157 ppm), so avoid breathing the dust.

name: Red iron oxide
relatedTo: Black iron oxide, yellow iron oxide, magnetic iron
notes: Synthetic red iron oxide is about 99% Fe₂O₃; natural red iron oxides (ground hematite) are weaker, about 76–95% Fe₂O₃ with clay, quartz and carbonate. A refractory stabilizer in oxidation until about cone 7–8, where it starts to lose oxygen and becomes a flux; in reduction it turns to FeO early and is a strong flux.
manufacturer: Potterycrafts Ltd (UK supplier; producer not named)
hazards: Synthetic grade: not classified as hazardous (Potterycrafts SDS P3441, rev 2025-10). Natural ore grades are labelled Warning, H373 (lung damage from prolonged inhalation) because they contain respirable quartz.

source.name: Potterycrafts Technical Data Sheet, Synthetic Red Iron Oxide P3441

name: Bentonite
notes: Wyoming sodium bentonite, the standard glaze suspender; 1–3% keeps a glaze from settling, but more makes it slow to dry and prone to crawling. It adds a little iron, soda and magnesia.
manufacturer: American Colloid Company (Minerals Technologies Inc.); also Bentonite Performance Minerals (National), Wyo-Ben
hazards: Danger: H350 may cause cancer (by inhalation) and H372 causes lung damage through prolonged or repeated exposure, because it contains crystalline silica (Volclay 325: quartz up to 6%, cristobalite up to 2%). Avoid breathing dust.

source.name: American Colloid Company, VOLCLAY 325 MESH technical data sheet (typical analysis, moisture free)

name: Veegum T
notes: A water-washed, white-firing smectite clay (magnesium aluminium silicate) used at 1–2% as a glaze suspender and hardener and as a plasticizer for porcelain and other non-plastic bodies. Hydrate it fully in water before adding the other materials. Vanderbilt publishes no oxide analysis for grade T; this is regular VEEGUM's, quoted in a 1964 patent, so treat it as approximate. It is magnesium-rich (MgO 13.7%), unlike sodium bentonite.
manufacturer: Vanderbilt Minerals, LLC
hazards: Not classified (Vanderbilt SDS 2023): no signal word. Avoid breathing dust; prolonged inhalation may cause lung injury.

source.name: Typical analysis of VEEGUM (R. T. Vanderbilt Co.), quoted in US patent 3,140,978 (1964); Vanderbilt publishes none for grade T

rawformula: SiO₂ 61.1%, Al₂O₃ 9.3%, Fe₂O₃ 0.9%, TiO₂ 0.1%, CaO 2.7%, MgO 13.7%, K₂O 0.3%, Na₂O 2.9%, LOI 9%
SiO₂ 53.2%, Al₂O₃ 0.8%, MgO 22.7%, CaO 5.5%, Na₂O 3.2%, Li₂O 1.3%, Fe₂O₃ 0.3%, LOI 13%
name: Macaloid
notes: A purified hectorite (magnesium-lithium smectite) clay, now sold as Elementis Bentone MA; it suspends glazes and hardens the dry coat without slowing drying as much as CMC. Unlike bentonite it brings magnesia, lime and a little lithia rather than alumina and iron.
manufacturer: Elementis Specialties (BENTONE MA)
hazards: Not classified (Elementis SDS 2016): not a hazardous substance under GHS. Avoid breathing dust.

source.name: Digitalfire: Bentone MA (alternate name Macaloid)

name: CMC gum
notes: An organic gum that binds and hardens the dry glaze coat, slows drying and helps brushing; it burns away in firing and is left out of the chemistry. Solutions spoil, so make small batches or add a preservative.
manufacturer: Ashland (Aqualon CMC) and others
hazards: Warning: may form combustible dust concentrations in air (OSHA combustible dust). No health hazard classification.

source.name: Ashland SDS, Aqualon CMC 7L Sodium Carboxymethylcellulose (SDS R0392869 v1.8), distributed by Laguna Clay

name: Epsom salts
notes: A soluble salt used in tiny amounts to flocculate (thicken) a glaze slurry so it stays suspended; it is a process adjustment, not really a glaze ingredient. Most of its weight is water and sulfate, which leave during firing.
manufacturer: Giles Chemical (Premier Magnesia); K+S (Laguna's SDS)
hazards: Not classified (Giles Chemical SDS 2020): not a hazardous substance under GHS.

source.name: Giles Chemical SDS, Epsom Salt, Magnesium Sulfate USP (magnesium sulfate heptahydrate 100%), with stoichiometry

name: Manganese carbonate
notes: Manganese(II) carbonate, a pinkish-tan powder; commercial grades are about 44% manganese (pure MnCO3 is 47.8%). Counted as MnO, about 57% MnO with about 43% loss on ignition as it gives off CO2 from about 200 C; gives browns, and purples to plum in alkaline glazes.
manufacturer: Various chemical producers; sold by Laguna Clay (US) and Potclays (UK), among others
hazards: Danger: H372, causes damage to organs (nervous system) through prolonged or repeated inhalation (Laguna SDS, rev. 2014-03; also the most common ECHA notification). Avoid the dust and vent the kiln.

source.name: Hitech-Chemicals, Manganese Carbonate Industrial Grade specification (listed for ceramic glaze use): Mn 43.5% min, typical 44.5%

name: Nickel carbonate
notes: Basic nickel carbonate, a light green powder sold at about 46% nickel. Counted as NiO, about 58.5% NiO with about 41.5% loss on ignition; the gas it gives off can blister glazes. Gives muted greens, greys and browns, and is used to soften cobalt blues.
manufacturer: Atotech (SDS distributed by Aardvark Clay, US)
hazards: Danger: H302+H332 harmful if swallowed or inhaled; H315; H317 skin sensitiser; H334 respiratory sensitiser; H341; H350i may cause cancer by inhalation; H360 may damage fertility or the unborn child; H372. EU harmonised classification adds H400/H410 (aquatic). Avoid all dust.

source.name: Atotech, Safety Data Sheet NICKEL CARBONATE 46% (SDS 2200984, version 1.0), as distributed by Aardvark Clay & Supplies

name: Iron chromate
notes: Sold to potters as ground natural chromite ore from South Africa, not a true chromate: about 46% Cr2O3 and 26% FeO, with alumina and magnesia. Very refractory; gives greys, browns with zinc, pinks to reds with tin, and blacks with cobalt.
manufacturer: Vibrantz Minerals (formerly Prince Minerals); natural chromite from the Transvaal, South Africa
hazards: Not classified under GHS (Vibrantz 'Iron Chromite Chromox 7901' SDS, rev. 2023-01, as sold by Sounding Stone; also Prince Minerals SDS for Laguna). Avoid breathing the dust; older potters' references call it highly toxic.

source.name: Zhengzhou Haixu Abrasives, Chromite Sand technical data sheet (South African origin)

name: Cerium oxide
notes: A rare-earth oxide used as a low-temperature opacifier and a weak colorant, giving cream to tan-yellow or orange especially with titanium or rutile. It settles quickly, so the glaze needs a suspender.
manufacturer: Various (rare-earth producers); SDS from PACE Technologies
hazards: Not classified (PACE SDS 2025): not a hazardous substance under GHS. Some suppliers list eye, skin and respiratory irritation (H315, H319, H335). Avoid breathing dust.

source.name: PACE Technologies SDS, Cerium Oxide powders (cerium oxide >99%, CAS 1306-38-3)

name: Spanish red iron oxide
notes: Natural red iron oxide mined at Tierga, Spain: about 87% Fe2O3 with some silica, dolomite and mica, so gram for gram it is a little weaker than synthetic red iron oxide. Bright orange-red raw; contains some soluble salts.
manufacturer: Promindsa (Productos Minerales para la Industria), Tierga mines, Zaragoza, Spain
hazards: Warning: H373, may cause damage to the lungs through prolonged or repeated inhalation, because it contains respirable quartz (Promindsa Micronox R series SDS, rev. 2015-01, distributed by Laguna).

source.name: Promindsa, EN 12878 CE label declarations for Micronox pigments (Micronox R03: Fe2O3 87 ±1.5%, loss on ignition 6.0%, quartz <3%)

name: Silicon carbide (fine)
notes: Fine silicon carbide (about 600 mesh, FFF) gives local reduction in oxidation firings, for example copper reds; larger amounts or coarser grits make bubbly, cratered surfaces. It is left out of the chemistry, though fully burnt it would turn into about 1.5 times its weight of silica.
manufacturer: Washington Mills (CARBOREX black SiC); others
hazards: Danger: H350 may cause cancer (by inhalation), because of a trace of crystalline silica (Washington Mills SDS 2025). Older supplier SDSs also list skin, eye and respiratory irritation (H315, H319, H335). Avoid breathing dust.

source.name: Washington Mills, CARBOREX black silicon carbide technical sheet (typical chemical analysis; powder sizes include 600 and FFF)

name: Stain (proprietary)
notes: Commercial stains are pre-fired, insoluble pigments; their make-up is proprietary and they colour the glass by staying suspended in it, so they are left out of the chemistry. Check the maker's notes for each stain: some need no zinc, some need high calcium, and each has a maximum firing temperature.
manufacturer: Various (Mason Color Works, Vibrantz/Ferro, Potterycrafts, Scarva and others)
hazards: Varies by stain: check the SDS for the specific stain. Mason's SDSs list many stains (e.g. 6600 Best Black) as not classified, but stains can contain cobalt, nickel, chromium, manganese, vanadium, praseodymium or cadmium/selenium (inclusion reds and oranges). Avoid breathing dust.

source.name: Mason Color Works: Mason Stains reference guide and stain SDSs

name: Crocus martis
notes: Crocus martis sold by US suppliers today is a micronized synthetic red iron oxide (Bayferrox 180) with a bluish-purple tint, not the old calcined iron sulfate. Use it like red iron oxide; recipes written for the old sulfate-bearing kind used more of it, because that kind lost about a fifth of its weight in firing.
manufacturer: Lanxess (Bayferrox 180 M), as sold by Laguna Clay and New Mexico Clay
hazards: Not classified as hazardous (Lanxess Bayferrox 180 M data; red iron oxide pigment). Nuisance dust; older Laguna SDS notes about 4% amorphous silica.

source.name: Lanxess, Technical Data Sheet BAYFERROX 180 M (Fe2O3 >96.3%, loss on ignition at 1000 C <0.7%)

name: Granular ilmenite
notes: Natural iron-titanium ore sold as sand-sized grains (about 30–270 mesh) to give dark brown specks in glazes and clay bodies. This grade is an altered ilmenite, about 64% TiO2 and 29% iron oxide; the grains do not fully dissolve, so the calculated chemistry overstates what goes into the glass.
manufacturer: Prince Minerals (now Vibrantz), per the Laguna and Axner SDSs
hazards: Not classified under GHS (Prince Minerals 'Granular Ilmenite' SDS, rev. 2014-10, distributed by Laguna and Axner); contains up to 0.5% quartz.

source.name: Axner Pottery Supply, Ilmenite Granular typical analysis (TiO2 63.50–65.20, Fe2O3 28.00–30.60, MnO 1.25–1.35, Cr2O3 0.07–0.12; 30 x 270 mesh)

rawformula: SiO₂ 53.5%, Al₂O₃ 16.8%, CaO 6%, Fe₂O₃ 4.3%, MgO 3.9%, Na₂O 3.5%, K₂O 1.3%, TiO₂ 1.3%, LOI 9.7%
name: Bentonit 57 (Carl Jäger / Bodmer Ton 507)
notes: Bentonite sold by Carl Jäger (Germany) and Bodmer Ton (Switzerland), and with the same analysis by Silica Nordic (Denmark): a swelling montmorillonite clay used at 0.5-2% (up to 3%) to keep glazes in suspension and to harden the raw glaze coat. It is much richer in lime (6% CaO) and lower in silica than American sodium bentonite (Volclay), so use this record when a European recipe calls for 'Bentonit'.
manufacturer: Not named; sold by Carl Jäger Tonindustriebedarf (Hilgert, Germany) as Bentonit 57/, by Bodmer Ton AG (Switzerland) as 507 and by Silica Nordic (Denmark)
hazards: Bentonite dust may contain crystalline silica (quartz or cristobalite); avoid breathing the dust.

source.name: Bodmer Ton AG technical data sheet 'Technisches Datenblatt Bentonit, Artikel 507' (Stand April 2025)

name: Bentonita (Prodesco)
notes: White, low-iron bentonite sold by Spanish pottery suppliers (Prodesco, Marphil) as a glaze suspender and plasticiser. The sheet gives it as about 80% montmorillonite and 17% opal-C/cristobalite, which explains the very high silica.
manufacturer: Not named; supplied by Prodesco S.L. (Manises, Valencia, Spain)
hazards: Contains about 17% cristobalite/opal-C according to the supplier; cristobalite is a form of crystalline silica, so avoid breathing the dust.

source.name: Prodesco S.L. Ficha técnica 50100200 'BENTONITA', v1.8

rawformula: SiO₂ 63.6%, Al₂O₃ 14.6%, Fe₂O₃ 2.8%, TiO₂ 0.4%, CaO 0.3%, MgO 2%, K₂O 0.5%, Na₂O 1.3%, LOI 14.5%
name: Bentonite Trubond (Miles, Queensland)
notes: Natural sodium bentonite mined and processed near Miles, Queensland; sold to potters by Northcote Pottery Supplies as 'Bentonite - Trubond' and used at 1-3% to keep glazes in suspension.
manufacturer: Unimin Australia (later Sibelco Australia), Miles, Queensland, Australia
hazards: Unimin TDS warns the product contains free crystalline silica (quartz). Avoid breathing the dust.

source.name: Unimin Australia, Technical Data - Bentonite Trubond (Miles Trubond 07/09), as posted by Clayworks Australia (archived)
